topic: Palomar: A Registry of Lean Verified Mathematics

key_points: Primary announcement, 18 August 2026, by Terence Tao; the canonical framing post everyone else cites.

Motivates Palomar by the recent proliferation of AI-generated proofs, some formalized in Lean, where verifying the repository actually proves the claimed statement is non-trivial for non-Lean-experts.
States the three problems a reader faces: proof typechecks, no 'cheats' such as extra axioms, and the formal statement semantically matches the informal claim.
Names the required repo artifacts: challenge file, solution module, formalization.yaml.
Describes checks (a) mechanical Comparator and (b) LLM judgement of informal-vs-formal match; stresses these fall well short of human peer review and that Palomar is NOT a peer-reviewed journal.
Tao reports he personally test-submitted his formalization of Sendov's conjecture.
Lists the scientific advisory board and links the Lean Zulip discussion channel.
The registry's own manifesto: since the start of 2026 the volume and complexity of machine-assisted proofs has risen substantially.

Problem statement: bold claims about machine-assisted resolution of famous problems announced with poor vetting, insufficient transparency, inadequate context, eroding what counts as an 'established mathematical fact'.
Positioning: role in the publishing pipeline is similar to a repository or preprint server (arXiv analogy).
Names the three Lean-ecosystem technologies: comparator, formalization.yaml, Verso.
States Palomar replays every exported proof through a second independently implemented kernel (nanoda) as well as Lean's own.
Signed by the full scientific board; jointly incubated by ICARM and the Lean FRO.
Definition: a public, searchable registry of Lean formalizations whose proofs have been machine-checked; each entry points to an immutable version of a public repository.
Details all three registration checks and the minimum standard, including the explicit research-interest floor (two questions the model must answer yes to).
States plainly 'Palomar adds no human editorial step: no one here reads the mathematics the way a referee would.'
Explains why review scores are withheld: the same commit scored 5 then 4 on one axis across two runs of the same policy.
No appeal exists for an individual result, by design.
Explains the public preservation fork and the allowed-axiom policy.
Describes what expansion to other proof assistants would require.
The practical mechanics: public GitHub repo, full 40-character commit SHA, immutable snapshot (not a branch or tag).
Exact required project files: lakefile.toml or lakefile.lean (+ committed lake-manifest.json), lean-toolchain, a readable Challenge module, a proved Solution module, comparator.json.
Hard vs preferred size limits for the Challenge source, and the transitive-import restriction.
Axiom rules: no sorryAx, no Lean.ofReduceBool, no custom axiom, no unnamed missing definition; assumptions must be stated, not smuggled in.
Points at the official starter template and a complete example repository.
Registration is permanent, append-only, and effectively non-withdrawable once registered.
Institutional announcement from ICARM (co-incubator with the Lean FRO), dated 21 August 2026.
Confirms the three automated checks and 'no human editorial step'.
Names the initial scientific advisory board, including ICARM directors Jeremy Avigad and Matthew Ballard.
States the strategic rationale: keep mathematics central, independently auditable, publicly accessible.
Maintainer-side launch post (Kim Morrison), more engineering-oriented than Tao's.
Frames Palomar as an index of repos with a valid comparator setup plus formalization.yaml metadata.
Explicit AI policy: 'Palomar doesn't have any opinions about use of AI' — entries range from no-AI to autonomously formalized, but the method must be disclosed.
Points at the interactive submission UI and its llms.txt for agent-assisted submission.
Origin of the 'But is it on Palomar?' catchphrase for social-media math claims.
Sharpest third-party analysis title/framing: 'Wants to Make Lean Proofs Easier to Audit — Without Calling It Peer Review'.
Explains the two-kernel design (Lean kernel plus the independent NanoDa kernel) and the exact allowed-axiom list (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound).
Notes the concrete submission limits (500 MiB checkout cap, 1000 lines / 100 KiB hard, 300 lines / 32 KiB warning).
Emphasises the statement/informal-translation boundary is where the LLM judgement sits and is the part a kernel cannot decide.
186 points and 39 comments: the main community critique thread and a good source of objections to address in the post.
Top objection cluster: the hard GitHub-only dependency (availability, single point of failure, other forges).
Recurring question: what is the incentive to submit? (answered in-thread by analogy to arXiv vs posting to X).
A 'recursive verification' worry — who verifies that the statement matches the informal claim? Resolved in-thread: you check translation fidelity, not the proof again.
Comparisons to theoremdb.org and to Metamath's centralized metamath.org set.
A concrete detail correction thread confirming Palomar keeps a preservation fork of registered sources.
First-hand practitioner write-up from a team that has actually submitted, including exact lake build and #print axioms re-verification commands.
Documents a real rejection: a submission cleared the mechanical gate clean and was then refused by the editorial review; refusals are private.
Documents an expensive filing error that cost a full submission cycle (~4h45m of queue and verification) despite correct mathematics.
Confirms the exact formalization.yaml basename requirement and the Challenge-only import surface.
Maintainer amplification on a professional network; useful only as a distribution/channel signal, no unique technical content.

stats.fact: Palomar opened for submissions on 18 August 2026, announced publicly by Terence Tao.
The registry is jointly incubated by the Lean Focused Research Organization (Lean FRO) and ICARM (Institute for Computer-Aided Reasoning in Mathematics).
Initial scientific advisory board: Jeremy Avigad, Matthew Ballard, Jaume de Dios, Nestor Guillen, Bryna Kra, Kim Morrison, Terence Tao, Ravi Vakil, Akshay Venkatesh (9 members).
Tao is one of four initial technical maintainers, alongside Matthew Ballard, Nestor Guillen and Jaume de Dios Pont.
Registry totals as of 2026-09-30: 383 registered results across 304 source projects (registry-wide totals from the data API, which counts every active version).

Home-page counters on 2026-09-30 read 346 registered results and 270 source projects, i.e. the registry roughly 6 weeks after launch; the 346->383 gap is the API counting all versions rather than newest-only.
Growth rate: the newest 200 entries alone span 2026-09-06 to 2026-09-30 (about 25 days), indicating a run-rate on the order of ~8 registrations per day.
Of 200 recent entries, 199 have trust level 'high' and 1 'qualified'; all 200 are status 'registered'.
Version distribution across 200 recent entries: 183 are version 1, 13 are version 2, 3 are version 3, 1 is version 4 — corrections are relatively rare.
Subject concentration in the recent 200 entries: math.NT 55 and math.CO 55 lead, then math.LO 25, math.PR 24, math.DS 17, math.MG 14, math.CA 11, math.FA 11, math.GR 10.
145 distinct authors appear across the 200 most recent entries; the most prolific are Arthur Freitas Ramos (18 entries), Michael Mislan (15) and JD Jones (9).
Current aggregate operating-cost run rate is $7,608.20 per year ($634.02 per month): OpenAI $6,008.76/yr, GitHub Actions $1,516.44/yr, Cloudflare Workers Paid $60/yr, domains $23/yr.
That cost forecast annualises the observed rate to 10,342 submissions, 6,388 completed reviews and 3,248 registrations per year — i.e. roughly half of completed reviews end in registration.

Palomar publishes an independent billing reconciliation: retained conversation logs reprice to $911.61 against $926.80 of OpenAI billed model cost over the same complete-day window, a coverage of 98.4%, and it refuses to publish a refreshed estimate below 90%.
Mechanical verification uses the Lean FRO's Comparator tool and replays every exported proof through both Lean's own kernel and the independent NanoDa kernel.
The current permitted-axiom set is Lean's three standard axioms — propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Disallowed: sorryAx, Lean.ofReduceBool, custom axioms, and unnamed missing definitions.
Challenge-source limits: hard maximum 1,000 lines and 100 KiB; the registry would rather review 300 lines and 32 KiB. The checked-out repository is capped at 500 MiB.

The Challenge module's transitive imports must resolve to Lean core plus the pinned, allowlisted Mathlib or Tau Ceti closure, and to nothing else. Dependencies used only by the Solution may be arbitrary pinned Git dependencies.
A project Palomar has already registered is not importable as a library on the basis of its registration — each entry fixes a reviewable snapshot of its own statement.
Submissions are pinned to a full 40-character Git commit SHA from a public GitHub repository; Palomar checks that immutable snapshot, not a branch or tag that can change.

Palomar keeps a public preservation fork of every registered source, purely as a registry backup if the original repository disappears (forks live under the PalomarArchive GitHub organisation with a commit-hash-suffixed name).

Registration is meant to be permanent: the record, the review, and the repository and commit enter Palomar's append-only canonical history. Withdrawal is not available once registered; only a new version or a lawful-request process, and a named Moderator may exceptionally retract one exact version with a public tombstone.
There is no appeal for an individual result, deliberately: reopening a few outcomes for whoever writes in would make the outcome depend on who complained.

The published review is redacted: it records that no blocking problem was identified and carries every comment, but withholds the scores, because the same commit scored 5 and then 4 on one axis across two runs of the same policy.
Palomar is explicitly not peer reviewed and its registration certifies neither novelty, nor relevance, nor complete agreement between the formal and informal statement.

The registry's editorial review includes a research-interest floor: a language model must answer yes to (1) could this warrant a research paper or serious note, and (2) can a credible research area and plausible researcher type be identified.

Registered results are searchable by arXiv category and MSC 2020 code, and the registry also publishes machine-readable data (CORS *, CC0) at data.palomar-registry.org with an API, RSS feed and JSON schema.
Tao's own test submission was his formalization of the proof of Sendov's conjecture, registered as PALOMAR-2026-08-13-000001.
The announcement thread reached 186 points and 39 comments on Hacker News, the largest single community discussion of the registry.

Palomar requires the formalization.yaml standard developed by the Mathlib Initiative, which has fields for recording collaboration, AI use (models and budgets), and adherence to social standards around licensing, referencing and attribution.
Main theorem rendering is automatic via Verso, the Lean FRO documentation system, which gives the entry page inline hover information explaining Lean terms.

An official starter repository (PalomarRegistry/PalomarTemplate) provides the layout, pinned dependencies, docs generation and CI checks, and the unit-distance example repo is given as a complete source-repository reference.

Submission can be agent-assisted: the submit site publishes its own llms.txt, and Tao notes modern AI agents are quite helpful with the mechanical details of a submission while human review is still strongly recommended.

Palomar currently verifies Lean only, but the project is open to other proof assistants and publishes the requirements an expansion would have to meet (pipeline, statement/solution separation, HTML rendering, dependency display, security review, CI cost assessment, and a 10-100 project sample).

angles: The registry is a refusal as much as a service: its load-bearing design decision is declining to referee the mathematics. Lead with what a Palomar entry does NOT certify, because that is where most coverage gets it wrong.

Two-kernel defence: Lean's kernel plus the independent NanoDa kernel, with the exact commit of each published alongside the entry — concrete evidence for readers who distrust single-checker verification.

The statement/informal-translation gap is the interesting part, not the proof checking. A kernel cannot tell you whether the Lean statement captures the theorem people are talking about; that boundary is handed to an LLM by design and is the honest limit of the whole system.
Why scores are withheld is a genuinely revealing design story: the same commit scored 5 then 4 on the same axis under the same policy, so the number was dropped as a judgement it could not carry.

Cost and scale are published in unusual detail for an academic initiative: $7,608/yr run rate, per-provider breakdown, and a 98.4% billing reconciliation that self-disables below 90%. This makes Palomar a rare example of verifiable-infrastructure accounting.
The research-interest floor is a mild gatekeeping mechanism nobody expected from an automated registry — two questions a model must answer yes to before a result is even registrable.

Practical gotchas beat theory for search intent: GitHub-only, full 40-char SHA, immutable snapshot, 1,000-line Challenge hard cap, Challenge imports restricted to core/Mathlib/Tau Ceti, and a filing error that can cost a full ~4h45m submission cycle.
Permanence cuts both ways: append-only by design, no withdrawal after registration, no appeal, and version URLs that must stay resolvable forever.
'But is it on Palomar?' — the maintainers' own social-media catchphrase is becoming a de facto trust marker for AI-era math claims, which is a strong narrative hook.

Address the GitHub-only criticism head-on: Palomar uses GitHub as a costless immutable datastore and forks every registered source into a preservation archive, so it is less fragile than the first wave of Hacker News commentary assumed.

Position against neighbours honestly: arXiv-like in role but not a preprint server; complementary to Mathlib, Tau Ceti, CSLib, Hex and Reservoir; distinct from theoremdb.org, which lacks the Comparator/formalization.yaml gate.
